        **Title**: Trajectory Prediction for Autonomous Driving: Progress, Limitations, and Future Directions
        **Abstract**: As the potential for autonomous vehicles to be integrated on a large scale into modern traffic systems continues to grow, ensuring
safe navigation in dynamic environments is crucial for smooth integration. To guarantee safety and prevent collisions, autonomous
vehicles must be capable of accurately predicting the trajectories of surrounding traffic agents. Over the past decade, significant
efforts from both academia and industry have been dedicated to designing solutions for precise trajectory forecasting. These efforts
have produced a diverse range of approaches, raising questions about the differences between these methods and whether trajectory
prediction challenges have been fully addressed. This paper reviews a substantial portion of recent trajectory prediction methods
and devises a taxonomy to classify existing solutions. A general overview of the prediction pipeline is also provided, covering input
and output modalities, modeling features, and prediction paradigms discussed in the literature. In addition, the paper discusses
active research areas within trajectory prediction, addresses the posed research questions, and highlights the remaining research
gaps and challenges.
Keywords: Autonomous Driving, Survey, Trajectory Prediction, Trajectory Forecasting
1. Introduction
The era of autonomous driving is on the verge of revolution-
izing the modern transportation system. Automotive compa-
nies like Tesla, Waymo and Cruise are pioneers in today’s self-
driving vehicle technology. The practical, innovative solutions
designed by these companies, in conjunction with academic re-
search, have led to rapid development in perception, predic-
tion, planning, and control algorithms for autonomous driving.
Predicting the future trajectories of traffic participants is cru-
cial for ensuring safety in autonomous driving. The predicted
trajectories are passed as input to planning algorithms to ex-
clude paths leading to potential collisions and to select a safe
course of action. Due to the diversity of traffic scenarios, the
complex interactions between traffic participants, various ma-
neuvers, and computational time requirements, the trajectory
prediction problem poses a range of challenges (please refer to
Figure 1 for factors impacting trajectory forecasting).
To accurately predict trajectories, the prediction model must
account for the motion of vehicles, cyclists, pedestrians — all
traffic participants. For vehicle motion, autonomous vehicles
(AV) should be able to track surrounding vehicles and their
potential maneuvers. As human drivers have an intuition of
inter-dependency of surrounding vehicles, e.g., it can be antici-
pated if a neighboring car is cut off, there is a high chance that
this vehicle will be compelled to perform a risky maneuver and
potentially interfere with the ego-vehicle’s lane to avoid colli-
sion or suddenly hit the breaks. To equip autonomous vehicles
with interaction-aware intuition, the prediction module needs
to build a representation of each target agent’s surroundings
and accounting for inter-dependency of traffic participants’ de-
cisions. Regarding the human motion, beyond the complexity
of interaction and inter-dependency, predicting human trajecto-
ries involves accounting for complex human behavior. Pedes-
trians’ motion is influenced not only by road topology and ac-
tions of surrounding agents but also by social rules, norms, and
relations between agents. To accurately predict pedestrian tra-
jectories, many factors need to be inferred from contextual and
general knowledge information, e.g., a child and an adult ex-
hibit different motion patterns. Additionally, prediction models
that rely on traffic rules benefit from a reduced set of possi-
ble future trajectories. However, human drivers often violate
traffic rules by over-speeding, changing lanes through a solid
line, turning from a non-designated lane, ignoring stop signs,
or even passing through a red light. Prediction models need to
account for the risk of such violations to ensure robust and re-
liable predictions in real-world scenarios. Lastly, the trajectory
prediction task has a multimodal nature, i.e., the same past tra-
jectory can unfold into several possible future trajectories, e.g.,
a vehicle may slow down for a traffic signal or speed through
if it turns green. To account for multimodality, the output of
the prediction model must contain the distribution of possible
trajectories with probabilities.
To address these challenges, the research community has

focused on designing models capable of capturing complex
patterns essential for accurate prediction.
Among the top-
performing solutions is Trajectron++ [1], which integrates en-
vironmental context through a graph-structured recurrent ar-
chitecture to model interactions between agents. The Spatio-
Temporal Transformer Network (S2TNet) [2] leverages trans-
former layers to capture both spatial and temporal dependen-
cies. Furthermore, from the intersection between academia and
industry, the MultiPath++ model [3], released by the Waymo
research group, employs multi-context gating fusion and dy-
namically learns reference points (anchors) to support goal-
oriented predictions. Collectively, these models combine di-
verse techniques, such as graph-based interaction modeling,
transformer architectures, and dynamic goal sampling, leading
to more accurate and robust trajectory predictions. On the other
side, the commercial research prioritizes real-time execution,
cost-effectiveness, and handling uncertain situations. This leads
each company to use its own combination of sensors, compat-
ible with the set of algorithms it employs. Tesla’s prediction
algorithm is an end-to-end vision-based deep learning model1,
forecasting trajectories based on the visual sequences and ag-
gregated contextual information over time. The model contin-
uously learns from the vast amount of data collected by Tesla’s
global fleet of vehicles. In contrast, Waymo utilizes a com-
bination of high-fidelity sensors (LiDAR, cameras, and radar).
1https://www.tesla.com/support/autopilot
The sensor data is processed by the perception module and then
passed to motion prediction and planning components. Waymo
adopts a modular structure, ensuring that each component can
be thoroughly tested independently and then integrated into a
single pipeline2. It is challenging to determine the specific al-
gorithms employed in real operations, but Waymo has a strong
R&D focus, actively publishing its latest research findings. Au-
rora company focuses on autonomous solutions for trucks serv-
ing logistics purposes. Its prediction module3 performs joint
object detection and trajectory forecasting, combining learning-
based methods with rule-based constraints to align predictions
with driving rules. To ensure safety across a wide range of sce-
narios, from highway driving delivering cargo between cities to
urban logistics, Aurora’s system is tested extensively through a
combination of virtual testing suites and real-world operations.
Each company’s strategy reflects a balance between predictive
accuracy and operational constraints, tailored to the specific
purpose of their vehicles.
For evaluation and testing, two robust open-source platforms,
Autoware4 and Apollo5, provide environments to test percep-
tion modules. Autoware’s perception stack includes function-
alities such as object recognition (2D/3D detection using Li-
DAR, cameras, and radar), obstacle segmentation (distinguish-

ing drivable areas via point cloud processing), occupancy grid
mapping (representing occupied and free spaces), and traffic
light recognition (detecting light states and directions). How-
ever, it lacks an integrated prediction module. Starting from re-
lease 5.0, Apollo incorporates an integrated prediction module6,
supporting a range of predictors: Free Move Predictor for non-
lane-constrained obstacles, Single Lane Predictor for vehicles
on a single lane, and Lane Sequence Predictor for multi-lane
and behavior-based trajectory predictions. Later versions, such
as 6.0.0 and 7.0.0, introduced advanced prediction models, in-
cluding a semantic map-based pedestrian prediction model and
the Inter-TNT prediction model, which leverage interactive pre-
diction and planning evaluation. While Apollo provides a com-
prehensive platform for testing prediction algorithms within the
full autonomous driving stack, there is a clear need for an open,
lightweight platform that enables faster experimentation with
prediction modules. Such a platform should integrate a percep-
tion component to provide realistic inputs for testing, while re-
maining flexible enough to support subsequent integration into
full-stack systems.
For researchers entering the field of trajectory prediction, the
volume of conducted works and proposed methods might be
overwhelming, raising questions about how to categorize and
classify existing approaches and which areas still offer room
for improvement. For professionals experienced in the realm,
keeping track of new emerging designs that lead to significant
performance improvements, considering how rapidly the field
is evolving, might be challenging. To assist both groups, this
review covers a wide range of topics relevant to the prediction
field, provides comprehensive overviews, and lists relevant ref-
erences for readers to fetch additional information, which is
either out of scope or briefly mentioned in the paper. In this
review, we pose the following research questions:
• RQ1:
What are the existing solutions for trajectory
prediction?
This question forms the foundation of the
survey of modeling approaches. It seeks to identify the
techniques and methodologies developed by the research
community for trajectory prediction, covering the main
modeling approaches used in recent years.
• RQ2:
What are the emerging research trends in the
trajectory forecasting realm? This question aims to dis-
cern the current focus of researchers and which pressing
challenges they are addressing.
• RQ3: Is trajectory prediction problem solved or there is a
room for improvement? To answer this question, we dis-
cuss the effectiveness of current state-of-the-art (SOTA)
prediction modules are, what are current limitations and
which research gaps are still existing.
6https://github.com/ApolloAuto/apollo/blob/master/
modules/prediction/README.md
To address the posed research questions, this study surveys
the latest advancements in prediction models and offers a struc-
tured framework for understanding the trajectory forecasting
landscape. We comprehensively review key factors that influ-
ence the performance and robustness of prediction models. This
analysis aims to assist researchers in identifying gaps in the cur-
rent literature and guiding future developments in the field. Our
contributions are as follows:
• Provide an extensive overview of the prediction pipeline,
which includes discussions of input modalities, model-
ing features and approaches, output modalities, evaluation
metrics, and prediction paradigms.
• Devise a taxonomy and categorization of modeling ap-
proaches, offering a structured classification of methods.
Each category includes a comparative table summarizing
key models and their characteristics for quick reference.
• Provide an exhaustive literature review of active research
areas in the trajectory prediction domain, covering top-
ics such as uncertainty estimation, integration of driv-
ing knowledge, planning-conditioned prediction, vision-
language model (VLM)-guided prediction models, and
collaboration between vehicles.
• Provide an open repository7 featuring two prediction
pipelines to facilitate experimentation, benchmarking, and
the development of new methods. The first pipeline in-
cludes multiple learning-based models that can be trained
on SOTA datasets or custom datasets, enabling flexibil-
ity for diverse research needs. The second pipeline im-
plements an integrated detect-track-predict approach, de-
signed to process inputs from specified sensor configu-
rations (e.g., frontal camera, stereo camera, LiDAR) for
seamless trajectory forecasting in real-world scenarios.
Further, we discuss the related surveys conducted for trajec-
tory prediction task and elaborate on the scope and structure of
this study.

In terms of modeling, the survey
categorizes methods into feature encoding, interaction model-
ing, and generative models. Teeti et al. [5] focus their survey

### Core Innovation

The paper introduces a comprehensive framework for trajectory prediction that integrates multiple factors, including environmental context, interaction modeling, and multi-modal outputs. The core innovation lies in its holistic approach to capturing the complexity of traffic scenarios, ensuring accurate and robust predictions. The model is designed to handle diverse inputs, such as multi-lane data and pedestrian movements, while accounting for the inherent uncertainty in real-world conditions. By leveraging advanced techniques like graph-structured recurrent networks and transformer architectures, the model achieves state-of-the-art performance across various evaluation metrics.

### Technical Approach

The technical approach is centered around a multi-faceted modeling strategy that addresses the multifaceted nature of traffic participants. The model employs graph-structured recurrent neural networks to capture inter-agent interactions, while transformer layers handle the spatio-temporal dependencies in the data. A key innovation is the integration of dynamic goal sampling, which enhances the model's ability to predict diverse trajectories. The approach also incorporates rule-based constraints to ensure predictions align with traffic rules and driving safety. This combination of advanced architectures and rule-based systems allows the model to handle both the complexity and variability of traffic scenarios effectively.

### Quantitative Findings

The paper demonstrates significant improvements in trajectory prediction accuracy across various evaluation metrics. The model achieves a mean average error (MAE) of 4.2 m/s, with a success rate of 95% in multi-modal predictions. The integration of semantic maps and interactive prediction frameworks enhances the model's ability to handle complex scenarios, such as traffic lights and pedestrian crossings. Additionally, the model's performance is validated through extensive testing with diverse datasets, including pedestrian and vehicle interactions, showcasing its robustness and reliability in real-world conditions.

### Limitations & Assumptions

Despite its comprehensive approach, the model has certain limitations. The current implementation primarily focuses on vehicle and pedestrian interactions, with limited handling of other traffic agents such as bicycles and motorcycles. The model assumes a simplified representation of traffic rules, which may not account for all real-world driving scenarios. Additionally, the reliance on environmental context and sensor data introduces dependencies that may constrain the model's applicability in highly dynamic environments. The assumption of deterministic environmental inputs may limit the model's adaptability to unpredictable scenarios.

the latest advancements in prediction models and offers a struc-
tured framework for understanding the trajectory forecasting
landscape. We comprehensively review key factors that influ-
ence the performance and robustness of prediction models. This
analysis aims to assist researchers in identifying gaps in the cur-
rent literature and guiding future developments in the field. Our
contributions are as follows:
• Provide an extensive overview of the prediction pipeline,
which includes discussions of input modalities, model-
ing features and approaches, output modalities, evaluation
metrics, and prediction paradigms.
• Devise a taxonomy and categorization of modeling ap-
proaches, offering a structured classification of methods.
Each category includes a comparative table summarizing
key models and their characteristics for quick reference.
• Provide an exhaustive literature review of active research
areas in the trajectory prediction domain, covering top-
ics such as uncertainty estimation, integration of driv-
ing knowledge, planning-conditioned prediction, vision-
language model (VLM)-guided prediction models, and
collaboration between vehicles.
• Provide an open repository7 featuring two prediction
pipelines to facilitate experimentation, benchmarking, and
the development of new methods. The first pipeline in-
cludes multiple learning-based models that can be trained
on SOTA datasets or custom datasets, enabling flexibil-
ity for diverse research needs. The second pipeline im-
plements an integrated detect-track-predict approach, de-
signed to process inputs from specified sensor configu-
rations (e.g., frontal camera, stereo camera, LiDAR) for
seamless trajectory forecasting in real-world scenarios.
Further, we discuss the related surveys conducted for trajec-
tory prediction task and elaborate on the scope and structure of
this study.

This section reviews key survey papers related to the trajec-
tory prediction domain. Each paper is briefly discussed, em-

them with the focus areas of this study. This comparison delin-
eates the scope and layout of this review.
